blocks.prompt: The Rock That Turns Into Light
blocks.text: Space is full of little rocks. Most of them are as small as a grain of sand. Earth moves fast, and it runs into these rocks all the time. When a rock hits the air above us, it is going so fast that the air squeezes in front of it. The squeezed air gets very hot. The rock gets hot too. It starts to glow, and we see a bright streak. That streak is called a meteor. People call it a shooting star, but no star is falling. Almost every one of these rocks burns up high in the sky. It never reaches the ground.

blocks.prompt: The Rock With Three Names
blocks.text:
A meteor has three names, and which one you use depends on where the rock is.

Out in space, the rock is called a meteoroid. Most meteoroids are tiny. A lot of them are no bigger than a pebble, and many are the size of a grain of sand.

When Earth runs into one, the meteoroid slams into our air at a huge speed. The air in front of it gets squeezed hard, and squeezed air gets hot. The rock heats up until it glows white. That streak of light is the meteor. The rock itself is small, but the glowing trail can be seen from far away.

Almost every meteoroid burns away completely, about 50 miles above the ground. But once in a while a piece is big enough to survive the fall and land. Once it is on the ground, it gets its third name. It is a meteorite, and you can hold it in your hand.

Some nights you can see many meteors in one hour. That is a meteor shower. It happens when Earth passes through a trail of dust left behind by a comet.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in a full sentence.

What makes the rock heat up and glow?
What is the difference between a meteor and a meteorite?
Why do you think a meteor shower happens on the same nights each year?
answers: a meteoroid
the air in front of it gets squeezed hard, and squeezed air gets hot
a meteor is the streak of light in the sky; a meteorite is a piece that lands on the ground
(inference: Earth goes around the sun on the same path, so it crosses the same comet dust trail at the same time each year)

blocks.prompt: Why a Pea Can Light Up the Sky
blocks.text:
Almost everyone gets this one wrong, including a lot of adults. A meteor does not glow because of friction, the way your hands warm up when you rub them together. It glows because of squeezing.

A meteoroid enters Earth's atmosphere at somewhere between 25,000 and 160,000 miles per hour. Nothing that fast can politely push the air aside. The air piles up in front of the rock and gets compressed into a thin, violently hot cushion. Compressed air heats up. This cushion can reach thousands of degrees, and it cooks the rock from the outside in. The surface of the meteoroid boils away into glowing gas. Scientists call that process ablation. What you see streaking overhead is mostly that vaporized rock and the glowing air around it, not the rock itself.

Now think about the size. A meteor bright enough to make you gasp is often no bigger than a pea. It is visible because it is burning at around 50 to 60 miles up, and hot gas that high can be seen for hundreds of miles.

During a meteor shower, all the meteors seem to fan out from one point in the sky, called the radiant. They are not really fanning out. They are falling in parallel lines, and perspective makes them look like they spread. It is the same reason railroad tracks seem to meet in the distance.

Earth sweeps up something like 50 tons of space dust and rock every single day. Almost all of it never reaches you. It becomes light.

Earth collects about 50 tons of space material daily, yet you have probably never been hit by any of it. Why not?
answers: (the air in front gets compressed into a hot cushion, and the hot air cooks the rock)
(it is burning 50 to 60 miles up, and the glowing gas around it is much bigger than the rock)
(the point a shower's meteors seem to spread from; they actually fall in parallel lines and perspective fools the eye)
(inference: almost all of it burns up high in the atmosphere long before it reaches the ground)

blocks.prompt: The Day the Sky Won the Argument
blocks.text:
For most of human history, educated people knew that rocks do not fall from the sky.

They were wrong, and they held the position firmly. Farmers reported stones dropping out of clear air, still warm to the touch. Scholars filed the reports under superstition. Stones came from the ground. The sky was empty. A stone in the sky made no sense, so the witnesses must be confused, or lying, or simply peasants.

In 1794 a German physicist named Ernst Chladni published a small book arguing that these stones were real and that they came from beyond the Earth. He was widely mocked. One reviewer suggested he had lost his judgment.

Then, on April 26, 1803, the sky settled the argument. A fireball crossed the daytime sky over Normandy, France, and roughly three thousand stones rained down on the town of L'Aigle. The French Academy of Sciences sent a young physicist, Jean-Baptiste Biot, to investigate and, presumably, to explain the whole thing away.

Biot did something better. He worked like a detective. He mapped where every stone had landed and found they formed a neat ellipse, exactly the shape a scattering shower from a single point would make. He noted that the stones were unlike any rock in the local ground. He interviewed dozens of witnesses of different ages, jobs, and politics, people with no reason to agree with each other, and their accounts matched. His report was not a theory. It was evidence, and it ended the debate.

That mattered more than it might sound. Meteorites turned out to be the oldest solid objects anyone can hold. Most of them formed about 4.6 billion years ago, when the solar system was still assembling, before Earth had a surface worth the name. Earth's own oldest rocks have been melted, crushed, and recycled by the planet's restless crust. Meteorites were never processed. They have been drifting, unchanged, since the beginning.

Every one of them is a piece of the original material, delivered free, by the sky that scholars insisted was empty.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Meteoroid in space, meteor in the air, meteorite on the ground
Entry speeds of 7 to 45 miles per second
Heated by compression, not friction
Chelyabinsk, Feb 15 2013: about 500 kilotons, roughly 1,500 injured
Oldest inclusions date to 4.567 billion years
More than 45,000 meteorites recovered from Antarctic ice

blocks.prompt: Three Names for One Rock
blocks.text:
Consider the word you are about to use incorrectly.

The bright line that crosses the night sky is not a thing. It is an event. Out in space, the object is a meteoroid, usually a fragment of an asteroid or a crumb shed by a passing comet, often smaller than a raisin. The instant it strikes Earth's atmosphere, the light it produces is the meteor. If any solid piece survives the fall and reaches the ground, that piece is a meteorite. Three names, one rock, distinguished only by where it happens to be. Very few words in English are that strict about location.

The physics is stranger than the folklore. A meteor is not lit by friction. It is lit by compression. A meteoroid arrives somewhere between 7 and 45 miles per second, and at that speed air cannot get out of the way. It stacks up into a shock layer in front of the rock, and gas that is compressed that violently becomes furiously hot, thousands of degrees within a fraction of a second. The rock does not so much burn as boil. Its outer skin vaporizes and peels off in a process called ablation, and the glowing trail you see is largely that stripped material and the shocked, ionized air behind it. The object itself is often the size of a pea. You are watching a pea write a line across the sky from 60 miles away.

Most of them lose. Roughly 50 tons of material arrives daily and almost none of it lands. Occasionally something bigger comes through. On the morning of February 15, 2013, an object about 60 feet across entered the atmosphere over Chelyabinsk, Russia, moving at roughly 12 miles per second. It brightened past the sun and detonated about 18 miles up with the energy of about 500,000 tons of TNT. Nothing hit the city. The shock wave alone blew in windows across six cities and injured about 1,500 people, most of them cut by glass while standing at those windows watching the light. Nobody had seen it coming. It approached out of the direction of the sun, which is the one part of the sky no telescope can search.

What survives is worth more than the trouble it causes. Meteorites are the oldest solid matter available to us. The oldest inclusions inside them date to about 4.567 billion years ago, which is how we know the age of the solar system at all. Earth cannot tell us this. Our planet melts and recycles its own crust, erasing its early record. Meteorites were never melted, never buried, never reworked. They fell out of the beginning and landed in a field.

Finding them is the elegant part. A dark stone in a meadow looks like every other dark stone in a meadow. In Antarctica, a dark stone on a sheet of blue ice looks like exactly one thing. Better still, the ice does the collecting. It flows slowly toward the coast, and where it runs into mountains it is forced up and stripped away by wind, concentrating tens of thousands of years of falls into small stranding zones. Teams walk those zones and pick up meteorites like beachcombers. More than 45,000 have been recovered from Antarctic ice, including pieces of the Moon and pieces of Mars, blasted off those worlds by impacts and eventually swept up by ours.

So the sky is not empty, and it never was. The scholars who once laughed at farmers for reporting falling stones were not short on intelligence. They were short on the willingness to believe an inconvenient witness.
